The Ground Substance and Hydrated Matrix

Dermal cells and fibers are embedded in the ground substance (amorphous extracellular matrix), a highly hydrated gel synthesized by fibroblasts that provides tissue plasticity, visco-elastic turgor, and resistance to mechanical compressive forces.

Its molecular architecture is organized into three key components:

1. Aqueous and Ionic Phase: Fundamental aqueous solution containing glucose, electrolytes, vitamins, and metabolites, essential for nutrient transport and waste clearance.

2. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): Unbranched polysaccharides composed of repeating disaccharide units (amino sugars such as glucosamine or galactosamine). They are divided into non-sulfated (hyaluronic acid, a macromolecule lacking a protein core with exceptional water retention capacity) and sulfated (dermatan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, heparan sulfate).

3. Proteoglycans (PGs): Supramolecular complexes formed by the covalent bonding of sulfated GAGs to a central protein core (e.g., decorin, biglycan, versican).

Bioconformation and Hydric Turgor: Due to the high density of negative charges (carboxyl and sulfate groups), GAGs create a strong electrostatic field that attracts cations (predominantly Na+). This osmotic gradient draws large amounts of water, forming a gelled network (dispersed phase in an aqueous dispersion medium) that fills intercellular spaces, stabilizes tissue hydrostatic pressure, and modulates growth factor diffusion.

The Hypodermis (Subcutaneous Tissue)

The hypodermis (or subcutaneous adipose panniculus) represents the deepest portion of the integumentary complex, situated between the reticular dermis and the underlying muscular fascia. It consists of specialized loose connective tissue organized into lobules of unilocular adipocytes, separated by fibrous connective septa (rich in type I, type III collagen, and elastic fibers) that anchor the skin to deep anatomical planes and convey major blood vessels and nerves.

Physiofunctional Profile of the Hypodermis

1. Endocrine and Metabolic Function: Beyond energy storage as triglycerides, the hypodermis is a highly dynamic endocrine organ. Adipocytes secrete cytokines and peptide hormones (adipokines such as leptin, adiponectin, and resistin) that regulate energy expenditure, insulin sensitivity, and systemic inflammatory responses.

2. Mechanical and Cushioning Function: Dissipates external impact and pressure forces thanks to the compressibility of lipid lobules.

3. Thermal Insulation: Reduces superficial thermal conductivity, limiting body heat loss.

4. Structural Contouring: Defines the volume and aesthetic morphology of anatomical regions.

Lipid Composition: The intracellular lipid fraction (90-95%) consists of triglycerides (triacylglycerols rich in oleic, palmitic, linoleic, and stearic fatty acids), supplemented by trace amounts of free cholesterol, phospholipids, and lipophilic carotenoids, responsible for the tissue's chromatic hues.

Comparative Histology: White vs. Brown Adipose Tissue

The hypodermis hosts two morphologically and functionally distinct adipocyte populations:

• White Adipose Tissue (WAT - Unilocular): Characterized by spherical cells containing a single large central lipid droplet that displaces the nucleus and cytoplasm to the periphery. Represents the primary energy reserve and main endocrine source in adults.

• Brown Adipose Tissue (BAT - Multilocular): Composed of smaller adipocytes containing numerous lipid droplets, a central spherical nucleus, and a high density of cytochrome-rich mitochondria (accounting for its pigmentation). Specialized in non-shivering thermogenesis via uncoupling protein 1 (UCP-1 / Thermogenin), which dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient producing heat instead of ATP.

Cutaneous Neurophysiology and Receptor Systems

The somatosensory function of the skin relies on a complex neuro-receptor transduction network. Sensory receptors convert mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli from the external environment into afferent action potentials, transmitted via peripheral nerves to the Central Nervous System for somatosensory processing.

Physiological Classification of Receptors

Based on the transduced stimulus modality, sensory endings are divided into:

• Mechanoreceptors: Sensitive to structural tissue deformations (pressure, stretch, vibration);

• Thermoreceptors: Detect temperature changes via ion channels of the TRP family (Transient Receptor Potential);

• Nociceptors: Activated by high-threshold noxious stimuli (mechanical, extreme thermal, chemical);

• Chemoreceptors: Reactive to algogenic or pruritogenic mediators (histamine, bradykinin, cytokines).

Histocytological Map of Mechanoreceptors and Free Endings

• Pacinian Corpuscle: Encapsulated, rapidly adapting; detects high-frequency vibrations (80-400 Hz) and deep pressure changes. Location: deep dermis and hypodermis.

• Ruffini Corpuscle: Encapsulated, slowly adapting; detects skin stretch and tissue torsion. Location: reticular dermis.

• Meissner Corpuscle: Encapsulated, rapidly adapting; responsible for dynamic touch perception and fine tactile discrimination (10-50 Hz). Location: dermal papillae of glabrous skin (fingertips, lips).

• Merkel Discs: Non-encapsulated, slowly adapting (Type I); transduce surface details, contours, and static shapes at high spatial resolution. Location: basal layer of the epidermis.

• Krause End Bulbs: Encapsulated, spherical/ovoid, rapidly adapting; specialized in detecting light pressure, low-frequency vibrations, and negative thermal variations (cold sensitivity). Location: superficial dermis, mucocutaneous transition zones (lips, conjunctiva, external genitalia).

• Free Nerve Endings (FNFs): Unmyelinated (C) or thinly myelinated (Aδ) branched fibers; act as polymodal receptors for nociception, thermoreception, and itch sensation. Ubiquitously distributed throughout the epidermis and dermis.

Skin Appendages and Exocrine Gland Physiology

Skin appendages (ectodermal derivatives) form morpho-functional complexes integrated with the dermal matrix. They include sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine), sebaceous glands, the pilosebaceous unit, the nail plate, and mammary glands.

Eccrine Sweat Glands: Histology and Thermoregulation

Eccrine sweat glands are simple coiled tubular organs distributed ubiquitously. The functional unit comprises:

  • Secretory Coil (Adenomere): Located in the deep dermis/hypodermis, composed of clear cells (water and electrolyte secretion), dark cells (mucopolysaccharide secretion), and contractile basal myoepithelial cells.
  • Excretory Duct and Acrosyringium: Double-layered duct that partially reabsorbs Na+ and Cl- before releasing sweat onto the epidermal surface.

Biochemistry of Eccrine Sweat: Hypotonic aqueous solution (~99% H2O) containing electrolytes (Na+, Cl-, K+, HCO3-), nitrogenous waste products (urea, uric acid), lactic acid, and antimicrobial peptides (e.g., dermcidin, secretory IgA).

Neuroendocrine Control: Although part of the sympathetic nervous system, the innervating signaling pathway is uniquely cholinergic (mediated by M3 muscarinic receptors).

Secretory Disorders and Sebaceous Gland Biology

Pathophysiology of Sweat Secretion:

• Hyperhidrosis: Neuro-evoked eccrine hyperactivity caused by M3 receptor hypersensitivity. In the nail apparatus, it leads to keratin maceration, increasing the risk of onychorrhexis, onycholysis, and secondary fungal infections.

• Bromhidrosis: Malodorous secretion resulting from bacterial degradation (by Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus) of apocrine sweat lipids and proteins into short-chain fatty acids and volatile sulfur compounds.

• Oligohidrosis and Anhidrosis: Partial or complete absence of sweating, secondary to neuropathies, congenital factors (e.g., ectodermal dysplasia), or glandular aplasia.

Sebaceous Glands and Holocrine Secretion: Branched acinar glands associated with the hair follicle (pilosebaceous unit). Absent in palmar and plantar regions and concentrated in seborrheic areas. Secretion is holocrine: the glandular cell fills with lipids and undergoes programmed lysis, releasing its entire cellular content into the infundibulum.

Synthetic activity is finely modulated by the androgenic axis: dihydrotestosterone (DHT), converted locally by the 5α-reductase enzyme, stimulates cell proliferation and lipogenic engagement.

Biochemical Composition of Sebum:

  • 1. Triglycerides and free fatty acids (~57%)
  • 2. Wax esters (~26%, exclusive markers of sebaceous secretion)
  • 3. Squalene (~12%, hydrocarbon precursor of cholesterol with antioxidant properties)
  • 4. Cholesterol and cholesterol esters (~5%)

Epicutaneous Hydrolipid Film (Acid Mantle): On the stratum corneum surface, sebum spontaneously emulsifies with the aqueous fraction of sweat and intercorneocyte lipids, forming a Water-in-Oil (W/O) emulsion. This epicutaneous film regulates TEWL (Transepidermal Water Loss), maintains cutaneous pH within physiological acid ranges (pH 4.5 - 5.5), and provides an essential chemical barrier for resident microbiome survival.

Integumentary System (Skin)

The integumentary system covers the body and protects the internal parts of our organism. It is formed by the skin and other related structures:

  • Hair
  • Nails
  • Glands

INTEGUMENTARY SYSTEM STRUCTURE

SKIN (CUTIS)
  • • Epidermis: Keratinocytes (90%), Melanocytes, Merkel cells, and Langerhans cells.
  • • Dermis: Fibroblasts, Vessels, Nerves, Collagen and Elastin fibers.
SUBCUTIS

• Hypodermis: Adipose connective tissue that binds the skin to deeper structures.

SKIN APPENDAGES
  • • Glands (Sebaceous/Sweat)
  • • Nails
  • • Hair

The Skin

The skin is the largest organ in the human body: it covers the entire body and protects it.

Skin Structure

  • Epidermis
  • Dermis
  • Hypodermis (or Subcutis)

Skin Components

The skin is made of:

  • Cells
  • Little intercellular substance
  • Skin appendages

Skin Cells

  • Keratinocytes (90%) – produce keratin
  • Melanocytes – produce melanin
  • Merkel cells – for touch sensation
  • Langerhans cells – immune defense

Skin Appendages

  • Hair
  • Nails
  • Glands

In the Dermis We Find

  • Fibroblasts and other cells
  • Ground substance: water, hyaluronic acid
  • Fibers: collagen, reticular, elastic
  • Blood vessels
  • Nerves

The skin has a surface area of about 2 square meters and weighs roughly 3 kg (6-8% of total body weight). It is the organ that covers the body, protects it from external agents, and regulates vital functions.

The skin consists of two main layers:

  • Epidermis
  • Dermis

Beneath these layers lies the hypodermis (also called subcutaneous tissue), made of connective tissue.

What is the Skin For?

  • Protects the body
  • Regulates temperature
  • Senses touch, heat, and cold
  • Produces Vitamin D
  • Constantly renews itself: dead cells shed and are replaced

The skin is vital for health and well-being.

Caring for Skin Health

The skin can get sick. Possible issues include:

  • Infections
  • Allergies
  • Autoimmune diseases
  • Tumors

For this reason, it is important to:

  • Wash the skin daily
  • Use sunscreen
  • Keep the skin hydrated
  • Follow a healthy diet
  • Avoid stress and pollution

Factors like age, genetics, climate, and lifestyle affect the skin and can cause premature aging or damage. Proper skin care helps keep it healthy and protected.

Skin Functions

1) Protection

The skin protects us in several ways:

  • Mechanical protection: the stratum corneum and adipose tissue protect internal organs from impacts, shocks, and falls.
  • Physical protection: against heat, cold, solar radiation, and electricity.

To regulate temperature (thermoregulation), the skin uses:

  • Sweating
  • Vasoconstriction (constricts blood vessels)
  • Vasodilation (widens blood vessels)
  • Adipose tissue, which acts as insulation
  • Keratin protects against electricity.
  • Melanin protects against solar radiation.
  • Chemical protection: the stratum corneum and hydrolipidic film block acids, bases, and other harmful substances.

Other Important Functions

  • Immune defense: the skin helps fight germs.
  • Secretion and excretion: through glands, it eliminates sweat and excess substances.
  • Respiration: exchanges small amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
  • Absorption: can absorb certain substances (e.g., medicated creams).
  • Sensory: perceives touch, pain, heat, and cold.

Skin and Vitamin D

The skin produces Vitamin D via sunlight, converting pre-vitamin D3 into active Vitamin D (liver and kidneys complete the process).

Vitamin D is essential for:

  • Fixing calcium and keeping bones strong
  • Regulating cell growth (protects against tumors)
  • Supporting the immune system

A Vitamin D deficiency can cause problems such as:

  • Type 1 diabetes
  • Multiple sclerosis

Therefore, safe sun exposure and a balanced diet are essential.

This image shows the three layers of skin: epidermis (surface), dermis (middle), hypodermis (subcutis), along with appendages such as hair and sweat glands.

The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin, composed of several cell layers. Deeper cells divide and migrate outward, flattening before shedding. The main cells are keratinocytes.

The Epidermis

The epidermis is the outermost layer of skin, the part we see and touch. It consists of stratified epithelial tissue without blood vessels; it receives nutrients by diffusion from the underlying dermis.

Cells of the Epidermis

1) Keratinocytes

They account for 90% of skin cells. Originating in the basal layer, they migrate to the surface. Along the way, they:

  • Flatten out
  • Lose nucleus and organelles
  • Fill with keratin
  • Become corneocytes (dead cells)

Together, they form the stratum corneum, the skin's main protective barrier.

2) Melanocytes

Located in the basal layer among keratinocytes, they produce melanin (a pigment synthesized from tyrosine and transferred to keratinocytes) to protect DNA from UV radiation. Production depends on genetics and sun exposure.

3) Langerhans Cells

Present in all layers (especially the spinous layer), they act as the first immune defense line in the skin: recognizing germs and foreign substances to trigger an immune response.

4) Merkel Cells

Located in the basal layer and connected to nerve endings, they form specialized sensory units that perceive light touch and pressure.

The Five Layers of the Epidermis

Microscopically, 5 layers are identified based on the maturation stage of keratinocytes as they migrate upward:

  • Stratum basale
  • Stratum spinosum
  • Stratum granulosum
  • Stratum lucidum (present only on palms and soles)
  • Stratum corneum

The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis, directly contacting the dermis. It is called 'germinative' because its cells continuously divide to create new keratinocytes.

In this layer we find:

  • Young keratinocytes: continuously dividing
  • Melanocytes: producers of melanin
  • Merkel cells: for tactile sensitivity

Without this layer, the skin could not regenerate.

Detail: Stratum Basale or Germinative Layer

Composed of a single row of columnar keratinocytes with high mitotic activity: when a cell divides, one remains in the basal layer while the other migrates toward the surface, maturing. There is approximately one melanocyte for every 5-6 keratinocytes.

Stratum Spinosum or Spinous Layer

The thickest layer (4-10 rows of cuboidal cells). Keratinocytes are joined by cytoplasmic extensions ('spines' or desmosomes) providing high mechanical strength. It also houses Langerhans cells.

Stratum Granulosum

Here cells flatten and fill with keratohyalin granules, essential for the keratinization process. Combined with keratin, keratohyalin forms a waterproof barrier. Cell nuclei begin to degrade here, signaling the onset of cell death.

Stratum Lucidum

A thin layer found exclusively in thick skin (palms and soles). Composed of 1-2 rows of dead, flattened, translucent cells rich in eleidin (an intermediate compound of keratin).
en.tegumentario_sezione_2:
Keratin and the process of keratogenesis

Keratin is a resistant protein. It is present in skin, nails, body hair, and head hair. It is made of amino acids arranged in a helical structure. The most important amino acid is cysteine, which forms disulfide bonds between keratin fibers, making them strong and stable.

Skin cells constantly renew themselves. New cells are born in the basal layer through mitosis, then move up toward the surface. Along the way, they:

  • Produce keratin
  • Lose their nucleus
  • Flatten out
  • Become corneocytes (dead cells)

At the surface, old cells flake off. This process is called desquamation. An important balance exists:

  • One cell is born → one cell dies
  • Skin thickness remains constant

The time required to renew the entire epidermis is called turnover, averaging 25-28 days.

Melanin and the process of melanogenesis

Skin and hair color depends on melanin, a pigment naturally produced by the body. Melanin forms from tyrosine, an amino acid. There are two main types:

  • Pheomelanin: yellow-to-red colors
  • Eumelanin: brown-to-black colors

Eumelanin provides better UV protection, reducing the risk of sunburns and DNA damage. Fair skin has less melanin, offering less sun protection, but it helps produce more vitamin D3, which is essential for bones, teeth, the immune system, and hormonal balance.

How is melanin formed?

Melanocytes produce melanin through a process called melanogenesis. They are located in the basal layer among keratinocytes, possessing a star-like shape with many extensions. Inside melanocytes are melanosomes, small vesicles where melanin is produced and stored. Melanin production depends on:

  • Internal factors: such as hormones (e.g., MSH)
  • External factors: sunlight, diet, vitamins

When the skin is exposed to sunlight:

  • Melanosomes move into the extensions
  • Melanin is transferred to keratinocytes
  • It protects cells from UV rays (UVA and UVB)

Melanin acts as a natural filter for the skin.

The dermis

The dermis is the layer beneath the epidermis, made of strong, elastic connective tissue. It ranges from 1 to 2 mm in thickness and performs several functions:

  • Supports the skin
  • Keeps it elastic and resilient
  • Nourishes it through blood vessels

The dermis contains:

  • Blood and lymphatic vessels
  • Nerves
  • Hair follicles
  • Sebaceous and sweat glands

The dermis has three layers:

1) Papillary dermis (superficial)

The layer closest to the epidermis, featuring small projections called dermal papillae. These interlock with the epidermis, forming skin ridges (visible on fingertips) that improve nutrient exchange. It consists of loose connective tissue containing:

  • Thin collagen fibers
  • Abundant ground substance (fluid)
  • Numerous fibroblasts
  • Touch receptors (Meissner's corpuscles) and cold receptors (Krause's end bulbs)

It contains few blood vessels.

2) Middle dermis (corium)

Intermediate layer with less ground substance than the papillary dermis. Contains:

  • Larger blood vessels
  • Bundles of reticular fibers
  • Other sensory receptors

3) Reticular dermis (deep)

The thickest layer, forming 80% of the dermis. It is highly resistant thanks to:

  • Strong collagen fibers
  • Elastic fibers (elastin)

It features numerous large blood vessels and sensitive nerve endings. Located here are sensory corpuscles:

  • Ruffini corpuscles: sense heat
  • Pacinian corpuscles: sense pressure

The deep dermis provides strength and elasticity while helping detect heat and pressure via its receptors.

Cells of the dermis

The dermis contains several cell types. Fibroblasts produce fibers and matrix binding the tissue together, while other cells defend the skin against germs and foreign substances.

1) Fibroblasts

The most abundant cells in the dermis, star-shaped, producing:

  • Collagen and elastin fibers
  • Ground substance (e.g., hyaluronic acid)

These substances provide skin strength and elasticity.

2) Blood-derived cells

White blood cells that enter the dermis during infection or inflammation, supplying:

  • Granulocytes
  • Lymphocytes

They help combat pathogens.

3) Plasma cells

Produce antibodies that recognize and neutralize pathogens.

4) Macrophages

White blood cells that engulf bacteria, dead cells, and foreign material, playing a crucial role in immune defense.

5) Mast cells

Sentinel defense cells that detect bacteria and foreign substances, initiating an inflammatory response upon detecting threats. Plasma cells, macrophages, and mast cells form part of the immune system.

Fibers

The dermis contains two main fiber types: collagen and elastic fibers.

Collagen fibers

The most abundant, accounting for 70% of skin proteins. Highly resistant, they support the dermis and protect against tearing. The superficial dermis also contains thinner collagen fibers called reticular fibers.

Elastic fibers

Less abundant (2% of skin proteins), made of elastin. They provide elasticity, allowing the skin to:

  • Move with facial expressions
  • Return to shape after stretching
  • Adapt to body changes over time

Collagen and elastin work together: one provides strength, the other elasticity.

Ground substance

Cells and fibers are embedded in a gelatinous matrix produced by fibroblasts, providing flexibility and plasticity. It mainly consists of:

  • Water– in large amounts
  • Glucose, salts, vitamins, and ions– vital nutrients for cells
  • Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)– with hyaluronic acid being the most abundant

GAGs are long sugar chains that retain large amounts of water, forming a gel akin to a wet sponge. In this gel:

  • GAG molecules represent the dispersed phase (the network)
  • Water acts as the dispersing phase (filling spaces)

This gel occupies nearly all space between dermal cells, essential for:

  • Maintaining skin hydration
  • Providing firmness and plumpness (skin turgor)
  • Protecting cells
  • Facilitating nutrient exchange

The hypodermis is the deepest layer of the skin, located beneath the dermis. Also called subcutis, it consists mostly of adipose tissue with fat cells called adipocytes. Key functions include:

  • Protection: acts as a cushion against impacts and trauma
  • Insulation: maintains body heat
  • Energy storage: adipocytes store lipids
  • Connection: anchors skin to underlying tissues (muscles and bones)

The hypodermis also contains:

  • Blood vessels
  • Nerves
  • Connective fibers

Hypodermis thickness varies per individual based on age, sex, diet, and genetics.

The hypodermis

The hypodermis is the deepest skin layer beneath the dermis, extending to muscle fascia. It consists of adipose connective tissue rich in adipocytes. Between adipocytes are:

  • Collagen fibers
  • Blood and lymphatic vessels
  • Nerves
  • Sweat glands
  • Hair follicles

Functions of the hypodermis

  • Energy reserve: stores lipids accessible when needed
  • Mechanical protection: acts as a shock absorber against impact
  • Thermal insulation: retains body warmth
  • Body shaping: defines body contour and aesthetic appearance

Fats within adipocytes primarily comprise:

  • Oleic acid
  • Palmitic acid
  • Linoleic acid
  • Stearic acid
  • Cholesterol and yellow pigments

Two types of adipose tissue

1) White adipose tissue

The most common, accounting for nearly all reserve fat in the body. Characteristics:

  • Single large lipid droplet inside the cell
  • Flattened nucleus displaced to the periphery
  • Yellowish color (due to carotenoids)

Primary function: energy storage.

2) Brown adipose tissue

Brown adipose tissue contains multiple small lipid droplets and a central nucleus. Rich in mitochondria (“powerhouses” of cells) and blood vessels, its main function is heat production to help maintain body temperature. Highly abundant in:

  • Newborns
  • Hibernating mammals (e.g., bears)

In newborns, it is mostly found in:

  • Axillary region
  • Interscapular area (between shoulder blades)

With growth, most brown tissue transitions to white tissue. In adults, brown tissue exists only in small amounts, forming tiny islands within white fat cells. Pure deposits of a single type do not exist; adipose tissues are always mixed, with percentages depending on body location.

The cutaneous nervous network

The skin senses through a dense network of nerves. It contains many specialized receptors. They capture different stimuli and send them to the brain.

The brain transforms them into sensations such as:

  • Touch
  • Pressure
  • Heat and cold
  • Pain

Each receptor responds to a different type of stimulus.

The main skin receptors

  • Mechanoreceptors: sense touch, pressure, and vibrations
  • Thermoreceptors: respond to heat and cold
  • Nociceptors: sense pain
  • Chemoreceptors: react to chemical substances (e.g. irritants)

Receptors are not evenly distributed across the entire body. They are more numerous in the most sensitive areas, such as:

  • Hands
  • Feet
  • Lips
  • Face

In these areas, the skin is richer in nerve endings. For this reason, we perceive touch and temperature changes better.

Here are the main receptors of the skin and what they sense:

Pacinian corpuscle

  • Responds to pressure and strong vibrations
  • Located in the deep dermis and hypodermis

Ruffini corpuscle

  • Senses heat and prolonged pressure
  • Located in the deep dermis

Krause corpuscle

  • Senses cold
  • Located in the superficial dermis

Meissner corpuscle

  • Detects light touch and slow vibrations
  • Senses surface irregularities
  • Located in the fingertips and tongue

Merkel corpuscle

  • Senses prolonged touch and light pressure
  • Located in the epidermis

Free nerve endings

  • Sense pain
  • Detect temperature (heat/cold)
  • Sensitive to stretching and irritation

Skin appendages

Skin appendages are structures connected to the skin. They help the skin perform its functions. The main appendages are:

  • Sweat glands
  • Sebaceous glands
  • Mammary glands
  • Nails
  • Body hair and head hair

Glands

Glands are organs that produce useful substances. They release them through a process called secretion.

Sweat glands

They are present throughout the skin. They have two main functions:

  • Regulate body temperature
  • Eliminate excess substances (such as salts)

Each sweat gland has two parts:

  • Secretory portion (glomerulus): the part that produces sweat, consisting of a coiled tube.
  • Excretory duct: thin tube starting from the glomerulus that carries sweat to the surface.

What is sweat?

Sweat is a clear, watery fluid composed of:

  • Water (99%)
  • Remaining 1%: salts (organic and inorganic), vitamin C, antibodies, traces of urea, ammonia, and sugars.

What is sweat for?

  • Thermoregulation: maintains constant body temperature
  • Toxin elimination: helps cleanse the body
  • Acidic pH maintenance: protects skin from bacteria

Who controls sweat production?

The autonomic nervous system (specifically the sympathetic system) regulates sweat. The body produces sweat during heat, physical activity, stress, or strong emotions. About 1 liter of sweat is produced daily.

Two types of sweat glands

1) Eccrine glands

  • Present all over the skin (most numerous on forehead, armpits, palms of hands, and soles of feet)
  • Have a duct leading directly to the surface pore
  • Produce clear, watery sweat to cool down the body

2) Apocrine glands

  • Connected to hair follicles (only in armpits and pubic area)
  • Produce a thick fluid with fats and proteins (active from puberty via sex hormones)
  • Produce pheromones linked to interpersonal communication via chemical signals

Sweat gland disorders

  • Hyperhidrosis: excessive production of eccrine sweat (especially hands and feet)
  • Bromhidrosis: apocrine sweat broken down by bacteria causing strong odor
  • Oligoidrosis: reduced sweat production (non-congenital)
  • Anidrosis: total absence of sweat glands (present from birth)

Sebaceous glands

Present across almost all skin (absent only on palms and soles). Most numerous in seborrheic areas (scalp and face). Located in the dermis and attached to the hair follicle near the arrector pili muscle.

Sebum production and composition

Sebum is an oily, viscous substance composed of triglycerides, fatty acids, waxes, and cholesterol. Its production is regulated by hormones (androgens increase it, estrogens decrease it).

What is sebum for?

  • Emollient and lubricant: softens the skin and reduces friction
  • Hydrating and protective: retains water and forms an antimicrobial barrier

Surface hydrolipid film

Sebum moves up the pilosebaceous duct and mixes with sweat, forming the hydrolipid film. This layer protects the skin barrier. An excess can leave hair oily, hard to comb, or clog follicles.
